translations.translation: Moreover, it is also productive in ores of metals—copper and iron, lead and silver. Jet is also found here; the stone is a black gem. If someone puts it into a fire, snakes then flee away there.
observations: It refers to Britain, supplied by the preceding context; this context is separate from the exact excerpt.
The selected source says āres, not a silent substitution of a familiar ǣres form.
Generic man is supported locally; it does not inherit the ordinary lexical noun's complete productive syntax.
Gif introduces a condition with indicative dēð; ðonne correlates the consequence, whose flēoð is also indicative. No subjunctive is mechanically required by if.
Preserve the reported historical claim about jet without presenting it as a verified physical property.

translations.translation: Then, after a long time, when we raised our eyes from a distance, we saw on the island of Farne the father Æthelwald, dear to God, coming out of his retreat, so that he might watch our voyage and see what was happening to us, because he heard the crashing of those storms and of the surging sea. When he also looked at us and saw us placed in distress and despair, he bent his knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and prayed for our rescue and our life. And when he completed that prayer, he at once both calmed the swollen sea and stilled the storm, so that the whole fury of the storm ceased completely, and favourable winds brought us to land across the very calm sea. When we came up to land and also carried our ship up from the waves, the same storm immediately returned and came again. It had abated for a short time for our sake, and it was very great and strong throughout that day, so that people could clearly understand that the brief period of calm which had occurred there had been given from heaven, at the prayers of that man of God, for the sake of our rescue.
observations: The first sentence frames a temporal occasion, then supplies the main seeing event. Accept idiomatic restructuring of Ðā wæs ... ðæt ... ðā without erasing either event.
Gode is dative governed by lēofan; father Æthelwald is the accusative person seen. Do not translate God as the one who sees.
The ðæt ... wolde connection expresses purpose (Cook p142 note18), hwæt ... gelumpe is a dependent question, and for-ðon introduces the reason.
At geseah ... bēon the accusative actor ūs is understood (Cook p142 note22); supply the complete perception frame and the actual gesętte source form.
Wæs gebiddende and wæs blinnende can be rendered with simple past verbs under the original cross-referenced note. Do not impose a mechanical English progressive.
He in the calming clause continues the hermit as grammatical subject. A theological explanation must not silently replace the expressed pronoun with a new subject in the translation.

Tō ðon ðætte introduces the actual consequence of the calming; later ðætte męnn ... meahton introduces the consequence enabling interpretation. The final ðætte ... forgiefen wæs gives the content understood.
The storm's return confirms the bounded rescue episode; do not stop the translation at landing.
For intingan ūre hǣle concerns rescue/escape here; the final forgiefen means given, explicitly distinguished from forgiven by Cook note18.
An English past perfect in the last portion can clarify relative event order. It does not certify an Old English pluperfect system or a new Unit12 tense-sequence assignment.
